name: Wise-Anderson Protocol / 'A Headache in the Pelvis' (Stanford Protocol)
founders: David Wise, PhD (licensed California psychologist; 8 years as visiting research scholar in Stanford Urology; former CP/CPPS patient; National Center for Pelvic Pain Research; inventor of the internal wand, New Pelvic Pain Technologies)
Rodney U. Anderson, MD, FACS (Professor Emeritus of Urology, Stanford)
founded_year_range: 1995-2003. Wise and Anderson began collaborating in the mid-1990s, and their 2018 meta-analysis dates the 'new paradigm' to 1995. The protocol was developed over about 8 years at Stanford. The book's first edition was self-published in 2003, and the 6-day clinics ran from the mid-2000s.
delivery: device (internal trigger point wand, external Genie)
cost_summary: No prices on the site ('contact for eligibility and cost'). A single 2014 patient-forum report put the 6-day clinic at about USD 3,000-4,000, excluding travel; the yearlong audio course was included. This figure is unverified and likely out of date, and the current format is 2-day. Book about USD 20-30. Prices for the wand and the 60-day home program are not published. The clinic is self-pay; the pre-clinic urology evaluation may be billed to insurance.
mechanisms: myofascial / peripheral tissue (trigger points, chronic muscle guarding)
autonomic/nervous system dysregulation (sympathetic overdrive, "stuck in fight-or-flight")
mechanism_summary: The protocol frames CP/CPPS and related pelvic pain as a 'psychoneuromuscular' disorder rather than prostate infection: a 'headache in the pelvis.' Anxiety, stress or an initial injury leads to chronic protective guarding of the pelvic floor muscles. The guarding produces myofascial trigger points, shortened and ischaemic tissue, nerve irritation and referred pain. Pain then raises anxiety and catastrophizing, which drive further guarding (a tension-anxiety-pain cycle sustained by autonomic arousal). One mechanism is applied across pelvic syndromes in both sexes, but only to patients with the pelvic-floor-tenderness phenotype. It is a peripheral-plus-central loop in which muscle and tissue change is the pain generator, not a purely 'brain-generated pain' model.
roots: Travell & Simons myofascial trigger point therapy
techniques: Internal (intrarectal/intravaginal) and external myofascial trigger point release by a PT
Self-treatment with the internal Trigger Point Wand with algometer (FDA De Novo DEN100023, 2012; Class II), 2-3x/week, 5-10 min
Partner-trained release; personal trigger point map
Extended Paradoxical Relaxation (acceptance-based Jacobsonian relaxation), about 1 h/day; yearlong 36-lesson audio course
Cognitive strategies against catastrophizing and fear of pain
Pelvic floor stretches; avoidance of Kegel strengthening; advice on sitting, diet, exercise and sex
Immersion clinic (historically 6-day, 3-5 h/day, about 20-30 h, <=14 patients; 4-day in 2023-24; 2-day advertised in 2026), then about 6 months of home practice
60-day home program: 104 videos, about 620-page manual, about 30 h of audio
mainstream_notes: Developed in Stanford Urology and published in J Urol. The generic component, manual pelvic-floor myofascial PT, is guideline-endorsed (AUA IC/BPS; AUA 2025 male chronic pelvic pain guideline; EAU chronic pelvic pain guideline), based partly on NIH network RCTs that Anderson co-authored. The branded protocol, wand and EPR are not named in guidelines, and the intensive clinic remains a private niche service. The protocol was influential in shifting CP/CPPS toward the pelvic-floor/biopsychosocial view, and the book is widely recommended by pelvic PTs. Adoption is 'moderate' only at the component level; for the branded protocol itself it is limited.
insurance_notes: The clinic, devices and home program are self-pay. The pre-clinic medical evaluation (Stanford or a participating urologist) may be billed to insurance. Generic pelvic-floor PT and psychotherapy are commonly reimbursed.

key_trials.citation: Anderson RU, Wise D, Sawyer T, Chan C. J Urol 2005;174:155-60 (PMID 15947608)
key_trials.design: Retrospective uncontrolled case series, refractory CP/CPPS, MFRT + paradoxical relaxation >=1 mo
key_trials.finding: 72% moderately or markedly improved on GRA; scores fell by a median of 8 points when >=25% improvement was first observed (median 5 sessions)

key_trials.citation: Anderson RU, Wise D, Sawyer T, Chan CA. J Urol 2006;176:1534-8 (PMID 16952676)
key_trials.design: Uncontrolled case series, sexual dysfunction outcomes, ~5-mo follow-up
key_trials.finding: 70% GRA responders, with NIH-CPSI decreases of 9 and 7 points; improved ejaculatory pain, libido and erectile/ejaculatory function

key_trials.citation: Anderson RU, Wise D, Sawyer T, Glowe P, Orenberg EK. J Urol 2011;185:1294-9 (PMID 21334027)
key_trials.design: Uncontrolled case series of the 6-day intensive clinic, self-referred men
key_trials.finding: Of 200 enrolled, 116 followed for a median of 6 mo. NIH-CPSI -30% (baseline 26); 60% improved >=6 points; 82% GRA improved (59% moderate/marked)

key_trials.citation: Anderson R, Wise D, Sawyer T, Nathanson BH. Clin J Pain 2011;27:764-8 (PMID 21613956)
key_trials.design: Open-label pilot of the internal trigger point wand
key_trials.finding: 113 completed 6 mo (44 withdrew, none for adverse events); trigger point sensitivity 7.5 to 4; no serious adverse events

key_trials.citation: Anderson RU, Harvey RH, Wise D, Nevin Smith J, Nathanson BH, Sawyer T. Appl Psychophysiol Biofeedback 2015;40:45-52 (PMID 25708131)
key_trials.design: Single-arm cohort (6-day clinic + 6 mo self-treatment), Oct 2008-May 2011
key_trials.finding: 374 of 396 eligible. Medication use 63.6% to 40.1% at 6 mo (complete case); -22.7% in mITT

key_trials.citation: Anderson RU, Wise D, Sawyer T, Nathanson BH, Nevin Smith J. Appl Psychophysiol Biofeedback 2016;41:215-24 (PMID 26721470)
key_trials.design: Retrospective gender analysis of the same single-arm open-label trial (2008-2011)
key_trials.finding: 314 men, 79 women; median 3-point reduction in trigger point sensitivity in both sexes

key_trials.citation: Anderson RU, Wise D, Nathanson BH. Urology 2018;120:23-9 (PMID 30056195)
key_trials.design: Developer-authored meta-analysis of uncontrolled pre-post PT/biofeedback/CBT studies (includes the developers' own 2011 series)
key_trials.finding: 8 studies; weighted NIH-CPSI reduction of 8.8 points (95% CI 7.5-11.1), exceeding the 6-point MCID; no control arms

key_trials.citation: FitzGerald MP, Anderson RU, Potts J, et al. J Urol 2009;182:570-80 (PMID 19535099) [generic myofascial PT, not branded]
key_trials.design: 6-centre NIH feasibility RCT, myofascial PT vs global therapeutic massage, UCPPS (men and women)

key_trials.citation: FitzGerald MP, Payne CK, Lukacz ES, et al. J Urol 2012;187:2113-8 (PMID 22503015) [generic myofascial PT, not branded]
key_trials.design: 11-centre RCT, myofascial PT vs global massage, women with IC/PBS + pelvic floor tenderness
key_trials.finding: GRA responders 59% vs 26% (p=0.0012); pain, urgency, frequency and O'Leary-Sant scores not different between arms

controversy: All outcome data on the branded protocol come from uncontrolled single-centre series by the developers, who sell the clinic, wand, audio and home program. Wise is the wand's inventor and is affiliated with New Pelvic Pain Technologies, the patent assignee. The same 2008-2011 cohort is reused across papers, attrition is high, the main outcome is the GRA, and patients are self-referred and self-paying. The developers' supportive meta-analysis pools uncontrolled pre-post studies, including their own. There is no sham or RCT test of the protocol, EPR or the wand. Safety data on internal self-treatment come from one open-label pilot. The Cochrane review of non-pharmacological CP/CPPS treatments (Franco 2018) rated evidence for physical and psychological therapies as mostly low certainty. Pricing is not published. The model fits only the muscle-tenderness phenotype, and the clinic acknowledges that it cannot help everyone. A patient forum reports that Wise retired at the end of 2024; the official site does not mention this and still advertises 2-day intensives in 2026.

popularity.reach_estimate: About 10^5. There have been roughly 2-3k clinic attendees in total since the mid-2000s. Book and audiobook readership is probably in the tens of thousands to about 100k+ (Penguin Random House edition, ~500 Amazon reviews, 9 languages). There is wider indirect influence through pelvic PTs.
popularity.method_notes: The trajectory is anchored on documented events: 1995 founding; late-1990s forum spread as the 'Stanford Protocol'; 2003 first edition of the book; 2005-2011 J Urol publications and news coverage; Nov 2012 FDA De Novo grant for the wand; 2015-16 press releases and podcast (from 2017); 2018 Penguin Random House definitive edition (peak); shortened clinic formats in the 2020s (4-day in 2023-24, 2-day in 2026); Wise's reported retirement end-2024, with the clinic and podcast apparently continuing. Reach is estimated from clinic capacity (<=14 per clinic x ~8-10/yr x ~20 yr) plus book signals (~500 Amazon reviews, typically roughly 1 review per 100-300 buyers, and 9 translations). No Google Trends or Reddit numbers were retrieved, so the scores are judgement-based.
